steps.title: Spread the requests
steps.caption: Round robin deals requests to A, B and C in turn. Clients see one address, never an instance.
steps.body: Clients send every request to **one address**, and the load balancer picks an instance for each one. **Round robin** hands them to A, B and C in turn, so each of the three identical, stateless instances gets a third. Instances can be added, replaced or removed behind that address without clients noticing.

steps.title: Pick the least busy
steps.caption: Slow requests pile up on B. Least connections sends each new request to the fewest in flight.
steps.body: Requests are not equal. A few slow ones land on B, and round robin keeps giving B every third request, so its in-flight count climbs. **Least connections** (for HTTP, *least outstanding requests*) sends each new request to the instance with the fewest in flight, and the counts even out. **The power of two choices** gets most of that benefit by comparing just two randomly picked instances.

steps.title: Skip unhealthy instances
steps.caption: C stops answering /healthz. After 3 failed probes it is marked unhealthy and gets no new requests.
steps.body: The load balancer probes `/healthz` on every instance all the time. C stops answering; after **3 failed probes in a row** it is marked **unhealthy** and gets no new requests, while A and B take its share. The requests C was holding time out, and detection takes about *interval × threshold*. The numbers here are illustrative; each product has its own defaults.

steps.title: Recover and rejoin
steps.caption: C is fixed and passes 2 probes in a row, so it rejoins. Slow start ramps its share up gradually.
steps.body: C is fixed or replaced and passes **2 probes in a row**, so it rejoins. A **slow start** ramps its share up, so a cold instance isn't flooded the moment it returns. Taking an instance out on purpose (a deployment, a scale-in) works the other way round: it is **drained** first, which means no new requests while the in-flight ones finish.
